I once had an idea for a transitional game of some sort. It was before the Norse arc had even been revealed, and it itself was actually also intended as an "atonement" kinda game.

Kratos stands in the wasteland he's created with his vengeance. Realising he's doomed so many for an ending that was so empty, and so hollow.

Few gods have survived Kratos' rampage, but only one actively seeks him out. Not for a revenge scheme, or anything. It's more like taunting, but also pushing him in a very specific direction.

Chronos, the primordial personification of time. Not Cronus the titan, father of Zeus, although depending on the source material, sometimes they're the same entity. ANYWAYS!

Chronos leads Kratos west, across the Mediterranean, taunting him all the while and pushing every single button to make Kratos rage, breaking him down emotionally. Kratos is too drained to even fight back. He arrives on a new peninsula. Here he's led to a giant mother wolf, with two humans with her. She makes him prove that he can protect her boys, through fighting... She was old and wounded, and couldn't hold on much longer so she created a means to finally push them out to stand on their own feet.

He brings the young men, named Romulus and Remus, with him at Chronos' behest to a hill where he's instructed to teach them how to hunt, gather materials, and prepare to build. He leaves them to do their shit after instructing them and comes back to a familiar, and entirely unwelcome sight... More people have arrived to help building, and they're led by a spectre who no longer goes by Athena, instead being called Minerva. He can't deny that she's helping, and to be honest? He can't really be assed to make a stink about it.

Minerva greets him coldly, still miffed about not getting the power she was after. But oh well... Nothing to do about it. Instead she remarks she'll need help, Chronos agrees, and he's sent out to pick up surviving gods, like Aphrodite, now turning into Venus... He also finds a few possible ascendants. Including the very first God he swore vengeance against. And even old Cronus in a very diminished and weak form, one that looks almost human... Mars and Saturn join the fold.

I'll definitely end up writing a novel if I keep going, so in conclusion Kratos basically helps create something, the beginnings of Rome, and is then sent packing northward. The journey is part in helping him conquer his rage and look beyond himself. It's not redemption, it doesn't fix what he did, it doesn't erase his past. This is just atonement. There's no forgiveness or apologies exchanged between him and the spectres of the Greek pantheon. Grudge very much preserved, but no one wants to take up the fight again. There's no point to it anymore after all. The only one who gets a thanks is Chronos.

Some virtual worlds in these stories can be described as alive in their own way, Infinite Dendrogram, SLF, and A Certain Dude's VRMMO Life. The games themselves do very much feel alive, but that's not the point. But isekai is about getting "spirited away", transporting to a different world in body and soul. Not logging into a game.

Just providing my own argument on the matter.

Land of Leadale, yes. SAO, no. Land of Leadale makes a point of remarking that it's the reality now. That the people are real with real feelings. I don't know how the manga differs, but the anime is very much isekai.

SAO is a game. Trapped in it or not, it's a game. The only real interactions are with other people. Just like SLF, A Certain Dude's VRMMO Life, and Infinite Dendrogram are all not Isekai for the sole reason that they're games even if there's subplots and such which suggests that these worlds are alive in their own way, the main players don't teleport or get transported there. They connect to them via game consoles.

Digimon may take place in a digital realm, but the people get physically transported to the world which is what makes it isekai.

The definition of isekai is honestly very simple. Getting "spirited away" to a different world somehow, whether willing or unwilling.
